adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Blocked lookup is an exact, case-sensitive string match with no downcase/strip on either stored or checked email, so a spammer bypasses the block with a case or whitespace variant (e.g. Spammer@x.com).

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — The match_count/last_match_at write happens inside the User save transaction, so when a :block match fails validation the stats update gets rolled back and flows that call save/save! directly (e.g. User.create_for_email) record no trace of the blocked attempt.

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, the stats update happens in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (which calls `record.save`) and is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each` during validation. The diff itself does not show this running inside a `User` save transaction, nor that it would be rolled back on validation failure. In typical Rails flow, validations run before the persistence transaction is started, so the `BlockedEmail` save would not be part of (and thus not rolled back with) the `User` save. The claimed rollback/no-trace behavior is therefore not verifiable from the diff and likely incorrect.

Therefore, the claim that validations run twice per request—and that `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is invoked twice causing `match_count` to be incremented twice—cannot be verified from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count += 1 followed by save is a non-atomic read-modify-write that loses increments under concurrent attempts, and it lets unauthenticated signup spam turn every attempt into a DB write (or two).

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — The blocked check is skipped whenever an earlier email error already exists (uniqueness, whitelist or blacklist), so matching attempts leave no stats, and the ordering depends on validator declaration order in User.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email path is explicitly gated by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, so if any prior email validation has already added an error (e.g., whitelist/blacklist in the same validator, or presence/uniqueness declared earlier in `User`), `BlockedEmail.should_block?` will not run and thus `match_count/last_match_at` won’t be updated. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral coupling to validation order and it affects stats, but it may be an intentional choice to avoid overriding earlier error reasons rather than an outright correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — The client caches the email as rejected on ANY email error (e.g. "taken"), then shows a generic "invalid" reason for it for the rest of the session.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, on any failed signup where `result.errors.email` is present (regardless of the specific validation), the code pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (lines ~271-276). Later, `emailValidation` short-circuits if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns `failed: true` with a generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` reason (new block around lines ~65-73). Since `result.errors` comes from `user.errors.to_hash` (users_controller.rb) and can include non-“invalid” cases like uniqueness (email already taken), blocked, or not_allowed, the client will cache those emails as “rejected” and subsequently display the generic “invalid” message for that email for the remainder of the session.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is defined on the class prototype via extend, so every controller instance shares and mutates the same array.

adjudication.rationale: In `Discourse.CreateAccountController = Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`, the added `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` defines a mutable array as a prototype property. In Ember's object model, non-primitive default values on `extend` are shared across instances unless initialized per-instance (e.g., in `init`). This means multiple controller instances would mutate the same `rejectedEmails` array via `pushObject`, causing cross-instance leakage of rejected emails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — The validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and no spec runs User validation/save against a real BlockedEmail, so the transaction rollback and double counting pass silently while the suite stays green.

adjudication.rationale: The new EmailValidator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, which performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) during validation. In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, both examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the spec never exercises that side-effecting behavior. The added specs cover `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in isolation, but there is no integration-style spec in this diff that runs `User` validation/save with an actual `BlockedEmail` record to observe effects like repeated validation calls, or whether the stats update persists/rolls back relative to a failed `User#create`. This is a concrete test-gap/behavior-risk, not a proven defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — Returning user.errors.to_hash with the distinct "is not allowed." blocked message gives attackers an oracle to probe which addresses are on the block list and rotate around it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes UsersController#create failure response to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. The new `EmailValidator` can add a distinct `user.email.blocked` message ("is not allowed.") when `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` matches. Returning that structured per-field error lets a client distinguish a blocklist hit from other validation failures, creating an oracle to probe which addresses are blocked.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/user.rb:47 — validates :email, email: true` resolves the top-level `EmailValidator` constant from lib/validators/email_validator.rb, but the diff adds no require_dependency or autoload path for lib/validators (the other lib deps in user.rb use require_dependency), so the lookup may raise "Unknown validator: 'EmailValidator'".

The diff does not show any corresponding `require_dependency`/`require` or autoload/eager-load path change for lib/validators, so whether `EmailValidator` is reliably loaded is unclear from the PR alone. This is a concrete review concern grounded in the change, but the diff doesn’t prove it will actually break at runtime (Rails apps often autoload lib).

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — The users#create endpoint now uses `errors` for two shapes: a hash of field arrays here, and an array of strings in the RestClient::Forbidden rescue (line 214), so clients can't rely on one type for the key.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows users#create now rendering JSON with `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: ...` in the failure branch, but it does not show any `RestClient::Forbidden` rescue block (or any other place) where `errors` is set to an array of strings. Since the alleged conflicting shape is not present in the provided diff, the claim cannot be verified from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — The client caches the email on any `errors.email` entry (including "has already been taken") and then shows the generic `user.email.invalid` text instead of the server's actual message (e.g. the new "is not allowed").

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed create response that includes `result.errors.email` causes the entered email to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). Later, `emailValidation` short-circuits if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns a failed validation with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the server’s actual email error (e.g. uniqueness/"has already been taken" or the new validator messages like `user.email.blocked`/`user.email.not_allowed`). This means retrying the same email will show the wrong generic message and block re-submission without surfacing the real reason.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? does a case-sensitive exact match on email, so a blocked address resubmitted with different letter case (e.g. Bad@Spam.com) is not blocked since user emails are not normalized before validation.

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact match on the stored `blocked_emails.email` value (and `validates :email, uniqueness: true` also doesn’t enforce case-insensitive uniqueness). In the new `EmailValidator`, the raw submitted email `value` is passed through without normalization (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), so a blocked address can bypass the check by changing letter case if the DB comparison is case-sensitive.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — BlockedEmail.should_block? writes to the DB (match_count/last_match_at) as a validation side effect, so users_controller#create calling user.valid? then user.save double-counts every match and any extra valid? call inflates statistics.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is incremented by read-modify-write in Ruby then save, so concurrent matches lose updates; should use an atomic increment (update_counters/increment_counter).

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code loads a record, does `record.match_count += 1`, then `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb:14-17). This is a non-atomic read/modify/write sequence, so concurrent matches can overwrite each other and lose increments (and potentially last_match_at updates). An atomic DB-level increment (e.g., `update_counters`/`increment_counter`/`update_all`) would avoid lost updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is defined in extend() so the single array lives on the prototype and is shared by all controller instances and persists across modal openings.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a mutable array literal created at class definition time inside `Discourse.CreateAccountController = Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`. In Ember, such objects live on the prototype and are shared across all instances. Since the code later mutates it via `get('rejectedEmails').pushObject(...)`, this can leak rejected emails between controller instances/modal openings, causing incorrect `emailValidation` failures for unrelated sessions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any server email error (including "has already been taken" or a transient uniqueness failure) permanently caches the email as rejected client-side and shows the generic "invalid" reason instead of the server's message.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed create response that includes `result.errors.email` causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (line ~274). The email validation then unconditionally fails for any email contained in that array and returns the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` reason, regardless of the actual server-side error (e.g., `email` uniqueness `taken`, blocked, etc.). This effectively blacklists that email for the lifetime of the controller instance and replaces the specific server error with a generic "invalid" field reason.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? does an exact case-sensitive match and neither lookup nor writes normalize email, so a mixed-case variant (Bad@Spam.com) bypasses a block on bad@spam.com
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same bypass risk: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive exact email match without normalizing case, allowing mixed-case variants (e.g., User@Example.com) to evade an existing block (user@example.com).

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:10 — Unique index on plain email column is case-sensitive in Postgres, allowing duplicate case-variant rows instead of indexing lower(email) or storing normalized values

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.email` as a plain string with `add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`, which in Postgres enforces uniqueness case-sensitively. The new lookup logic `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` is also case-sensitive, so a stored blocked email like `bad@spammers.org` would not match `Bad@spammers.org`, allowing bypass via case variants and permitting duplicate blocked-email rows differing only by case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:5 — Model uniqueness validation is case-sensitive (no case_sensitive: false), matching the index gap and permitting case-variant duplicates

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail` validates `uniqueness: true` without `case_sensitive: false` and the migration adds a plain unique index on `email` (`add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`), so case-variant duplicates (e.g., `Bad@x.com` vs `bad@x.com`) are allowed by both model and DB. Since `BlockedEmail.should_block?` queries with exact match (`where(email: email).first`), this also allows bypassing a blocked email by changing case, which is broken behavior for an email blocklist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type is NOT NULL with no DB default, relying on a before_validation callback, so manual/bulk SQL loads of blocked emails (as the spec comments anticipate) fail unless action_type is supplied

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.action_type` as `null: false` with no DB default (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb), while the model sets a default only via `before_validation :set_defaults` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Any direct SQL/bulk insert that omits `action_type` will fail at the DB constraint level, so the schema default doesn’t align with the intended default behavior. This is a real operability/robustness issue but doesn’t break normal app flows that go through validations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is incremented via read-modify-write save rather than an atomic SQL update, so concurrent signups lose counts

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, the code loads a record (BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first), then does `record.match_count += 1` and `record.last_match_at = ...` followed by `record.save`. This is a classic read-modify-write sequence; under concurrent calls for the same email, multiple threads/processes can read the same match_count and overwrite each other’s updates, losing increments (and potentially last_match_at updates). An atomic SQL update (e.g., update_all/increment_counter) would be needed to avoid lost updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:4 — Generically named ActiveModel EachValidator in lib/ is hard-coupled to SiteSetting whitelist/blacklist, BlockedEmail and `user.email.*` I18n keys, so it is really User-signup policy and not reusable on other models despite its name/placement.

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) is named and placed like a generic reusable validator, but its logic is tightly coupled to signup/user policy: it reads `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist`, calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and emits `I18n.t(:'user.email.not_allowed')` / `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')`. This makes it effectively a User email policy validator rather than a generic email validator for arbitrary models, which is an architectural/scope concern created by this diff, not a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:11 — should_block?` is a predicate/query but mutates and saves the record (match_count/last_match_at), violating command-query separation so every `user.valid?` call writes to the DB and silently ignores save failures.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both note that the `should_block`/`should_block_email?` predicate has side effects: it mutates fields (match_count/last_match_at) and persists them during what should be a read/query operation, making the method misleading and potentially problematic (e.g., concurrency).

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — Blocked-email check is gated on `record.errors[attribute].blank?`, making behavior (and BlockedEmail match statistics) depend on the order of other email validators declared in User.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email path is explicitly guarded by `record.errors[attribute].blank?` before calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. Since `BlockedEmail.should_block?` also updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` (in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`), those statistics will not be updated if any earlier validator has already added an `:email` error. In `app/models/user.rb`, `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` is declared before `validates :email, email: true`, so presence/uniqueness errors can prevent the blocked-email check from running—making the behavior dependent on validation order. This is a real, diff-grounded concern, though whether it’s a defect is ambiguous (it may be intentional to avoid extra checks when already invalid).

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:18 — Helper `email_in_restriction_setting?` is left public on the validator instead of private, widening its API surface.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb the helper method `email_in_restriction_setting?` is defined as an instance method without a `private` (or `protected`) section, so it is publicly callable on `EmailValidator` instances by default in Ruby. This doesn’t break behavior, but it does unnecessarily expose an internal helper as part of the validator’s public API surface.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — Uses low-precedence `and` in a conditional instead of `&&`, inconsistent with Ruby style and error-prone.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, but in this specific context (a simple `if` condition with no assignment/chaining) `and` behaves the same as `&&`. The finding is essentially a style nit rather than a verifiable defect or substantive review issue introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:24 — File is missing a trailing newline.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly shows "\\ No newline at end of file" for lib/validators/email_validator.rb, so the observation is true, but it’s a formatting/style nit (missing trailing newline) rather than a functional defect or substantive review issue per the categories.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — Client caches any email error (including "already taken"/domain rules) and re-displays a hard-coded generic `user.email.invalid` reason, discarding the server's specific error returned in `result.errors`.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `rejectedEmails` cache and, if the current `accountEmail` is in that list, `emailValidation` returns a failed validation with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (create_account_controller.js:65-76). The cache is populated on any account-creation failure where `result.errors.email` is present (js:274-276), which can include uniqueness ("already taken") or domain/blocked-provider errors coming from the new server-side email validator. This means previously server-rejected emails will subsequently be marked invalid with a generic reason, not the specific server-provided email error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — should_block? writes stats inside the User save transaction, so for blocked emails the increment is rolled back when the user save fails; it only persists because the controller calls user.valid? outside a transaction first, and other create/save paths never record matches.

adjudication.rationale: From the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is invoked inside `EmailValidator#validate_each` during model validation, and it performs its own `record.save` on `BlockedEmail`. The finding’s key claim—that this write happens “inside the User save transaction” and is therefore rolled back on user save failure, and that it “only persists because the controller calls user.valid? outside a transaction first”—is not supported by anything shown in the diff (no transaction wrapping is shown, and no `user.valid?` call is shown in `UsersController#create`). The asserted behavior about rollback/reliance on controller and other save paths cannot be verified from this PR diff and appears to misread how the added code is wired.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — The validation has a DB-write side effect, so user.valid? followed by user.save in users_controller#create increments match_count twice for non-blocking (do_nothing) matches, and every repeated validation call inflates the stats.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a DB-write side effect inside validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s whenever a record exists, regardless of `action_type` (app/models/blocked_email.rb:12-18). That means any repeated validation (`valid?` called multiple times, re-validation on `save`, etc.) will inflate these statistics. However, the specific claim that `users_controller#create` does `user.valid?` followed by `user.save` (causing a guaranteed double-increment) is not shown in this diff, so the exact controller scenario cannot be verified here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count uses read-modify-write (+= 1 then save) instead of an atomic update_counters/increment_counter, so concurrent signups for the same email lose updates.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, when a matching record is found it does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a non-atomic read-modify-write update; concurrent calls for the same email can overwrite each other’s increments, causing lost updates to match_count (and potentially last_match_at timing). The diff introduces this new model/logic, so the issue is verifiable from the added code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — The return value of record.save is ignored, so a failed stats write (e.g. a validation failure on a legacy row) is silently dropped with no log.

adjudication.rationale: In BlockedEmail.should_block? the code mutates match_count/last_match_at and calls `record.save` without checking the return value or handling failures. If the save fails (e.g., due to unexpected validation/DB constraint issues on existing rows), the method will still return based on `record.action_type`, silently losing the stats update with no log. This is a real, diff-grounded robustness/observability issue, but it doesn’t break the core blocking decision logic shown here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:202 — Any DB error raised by BlockedEmail inside validation (e.g. blocked_emails table missing before migration, or aborted transaction) is caught by the broad StatementInvalid rescue and reported as "something already taken", which hides the real failure.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new DB read/write during email validation (`BlockedEmail.should_block?` called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which does `BlockedEmail.where(...).first` and `record.save`). That can raise `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` if the `blocked_emails` table is missing/not migrated or if the transaction is in a bad state. `UsersController#create` still has a broad `rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` (shown at the end of the hunk), so such failures would be caught and likely surfaced as a generic create failure rather than the underlying DB/migration issue. However, the specific claim that it is reported as "something already taken" is not directly verifiable from the provided diff because the rescue handler body isn’t shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Blocklist lookup is exact, case-sensitive `where(email: email)` on un-normalized signup input, so a blocked address bypasses the block via case changes or surrounding whitespace (e.g. Bad@Spammers.org).

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, and neither `BlockedEmail` nor `EmailValidator` normalizes the input (`strip`, `downcase`, etc.) before querying. This makes blocking dependent on an exact string match; if the stored blocked email differs by case or surrounding whitespace from the signup input, the query can fail and the address can bypass blocking.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and escapes only '.', so a whitelisted "example.com" also matches "x@example.com.evil.org" (whitelist bypass), and other regex metacharacters in the setting pass through.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core flaw: the email domain restriction regex is not properly anchored/boundary-checked, so a whitelist entry like "example.com" can be bypassed by using a longer domain containing it (e.g., "evil.example.com" or "example.com.evil.org"). The candidate adds extra detail about escaping/metacharacters, but still targets the same unanchored domain-match bypass.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — should_block? does a non-atomic read-modify-write save on every validation, and the unauthenticated signup path runs validation twice (valid? then save), so anonymous requests can inflate or race match_count/last_match_at.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail.should_block?` which does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` (non-atomic read/modify/write). This can lose or double-count increments under concurrent requests and also increments once per invocation of the validator (`EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`). However, the claim that the signup path *definitely* runs validation twice (valid? then save) is not shown in this diff; and the race/miscount affects stats fields rather than the blocking decision itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:14 — The distinct "blocked" error message, now also returned as a structured errors hash to anonymous signup callers, tells them whether an address is on the admin blocklist.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a distinct validation error for blocked emails (`EmailValidator` adds `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` when `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is true) and also changes the signup failure JSON to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` (and echoed `values`) in `UsersController#create`. This combination lets an anonymous caller distinguish a blocklist hit ("user.email.blocked": "is not allowed.") from other email failures (e.g. domain restrictions), effectively exposing whether an address is on the admin-managed `blocked_emails` list.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — Both validator specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so no test exercises the real DB lookup or proves a User with a blocked email is actually invalid via `validates :email, email: true`.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? (lines 9–20), so the validator spec never exercises the real BlockedEmail.should_block? DB lookup/update path. While spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb does test the DB-backed behavior of should_block?, there is no spec in this diff that verifies the end-to-end effect of `validates :email, email: true` in User (app/models/user.rb) making a User invalid when a matching BlockedEmail row exists. This is a concrete test coverage gap for the newly added blocked-email validation behavior, not a runtime defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:9 — Whitelist/blacklist domain logic moved from User into EmailValidator has no coverage in the new spec, and no user_spec change confirms the old tests still exercise the moved code.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves the domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic from `User#email_validator` (removed in `app/models/user.rb`) into the new `EmailValidator` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`), but the newly added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only asserts behavior for `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and does not exercise `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` paths. No other spec changes in the diff show continued coverage of the moved logic, so the finding about missing coverage is grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — No test verifies a whitelist/blacklist error short-circuits the blocked check (should_block? not called, match_count not incremented, only one error added).

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, the blocked-email check is explicitly guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, so whitelist/blacklist errors will short-circuit `should_block?`. However, the added specs (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) only cover the blocked-email branch by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and do not exercise whitelist/blacklist settings nor assert that `should_block?` is not invoked / match_count not incremented when a domain restriction error is present. This is a concrete missing-test gap for newly added branching behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — New `errors` and `values` keys in the failed-create JSON response have no controller spec, even though the client depends on their shape.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new response fields in `UsersController#create` on failure (`errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`), and the client-side code now explicitly relies on them (`create_account_controller.js` checks `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email`). The diff does not add any controller/request spec asserting this JSON shape, so a missing test coverage for a newly introduced client-facing contract is a concrete review issue (though not a direct functional bug by itself).

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — No JS test covers the rejectedEmails caching path (push on server email error, then emailValidation failing for that email).

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side logic in `create_account_controller.js` to cache server-rejected emails (`rejectedEmails` array, push on `result.errors.email` + `result.values.email`, and fail validation when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`). The diff also adds/updates only Ruby-side specs (for `BlockedEmail` and `EmailValidator`) and contains no JS test additions covering this new rejected-email caching/validation path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — No test covers case variants of a blocked email; the case-sensitive `where(email: email)` lets "BLOCK@spamfromhome.org" bypass the block, and a test would have caught it.

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization (e.g., downcasing) in either the model or the new EmailValidator. On typical Rails/Postgres setups, string equality is case-sensitive, so a blocked record for `block@spamfromhome.org` would not match an input like `BLOCK@spamfromhome.org`, allowing the block to be bypassed. The added specs only cover exact-case matches and would not catch this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:7 — No spec covers BlockedEmail presence/uniqueness validations or a nil/blank email passed to should_block?.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` with `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` and a `.should_block?(email)` method that queries by `email`. The accompanying `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb` covers default `action_type`, `last_match_at`, and behavior/stat updates for matching/non-matching records, but it does not test the presence/uniqueness validations nor what happens when `should_block?` is called with a nil/blank email. This is a specific, diff-grounded test coverage gap rather than a demonstrated runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:23 — be_false` in RSpec 2 also passes for nil (should_block? returns nil when no record), so the spec does not pin a real boolean return value.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when no record exists it returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, which evaluates to `nil` (not an explicit `false`). The spec at `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb` uses `subject.should be_false`, and in RSpec 2 `be_false` matches both `false` and `nil`, so the test does not actually assert a boolean `false` return value for the no-record case.
